reverse_outline.summary: Three takeaways: physical systems own their facts; promises must be computed from real inputs; each fact and view has a single source
Fast checkout still depends on slower physical picking, packing and collection that can delay delivery
Timeline of Eva's jacket order: late delivery, then a size exchange
Kestrel & Pine introduced with the scale of its fulfillment operations
Waypoint's three rules: single writer per fact, promises computed from its events, shared order record for all views
Roadmap: chapters trace the parcel out and back
Warehouse chapter: order-to-warehouse handoff, illustrated by a Black Friday backlog that never reached the floor
Shipping chapter: delivery dates must be computed from cut-offs, backlog and carrier data, not a fixed rule
Stores chapter: tills as order and stock sources, shown by a click-and-collect trial selling phantom stock
Returns chapter: separate states and owners for request, inspection, restock and refund, shown by double refunds
Customer service chapter: aligning all status views, shown by a split-shipment order generating tickets
Common diagnosis that promises came from the wrong source, plus a pointer to start with the warehouse chapter

The outliner marked the KEY POINTS callout as two ideas; it is the house-format three-bullet summary of the thesis, declared as evidence of p04, not a prose paragraph, so three takeaways are its intended form.

The outliner marked diagnosis plus pointer as two ideas; the spec's p11 controlling idea and the conclusion's synthesis and course_of_action takeaway declare exactly this pair for the one closing unit, and the pointer follows from the diagnosis.
Example paragraph; traces through the thesis's how_why (promise in seconds, physical work later) that p04 states.
Example paragraph; Eva's order passes the warehouse, carrier and returns bench whose facts the claim (P4-1, P4-3, P4-4) concerns.
Context paragraph; names the places (warehouse, carriers, stores, returns) that P4-1 assigns as witnesses.

Claim paragraph; states P4-1 (only writer), P4-3/P4-4 (promise computed from the writer's events, refund waits for the bench) and P4-5 (one order record). P4-2 is not stated, a gap the decision log records for length.
Transition paragraph; orders the chapters that argue P4-1 to P4-5.
Traces to P4-2 (work instruction and response) and P4-3 (backlog); P4-1 implicit.
Traces to P4-3: the promise must read collection schedules, backlog, location and carrier performance.
Traces to P4-1: the till as another source (witness) of stock; P4-3's staff confirmation is not stated but the paragraph still serves P4-1.
Traces to P4-4: refund and restock wait for inspection, one system issues refunds.
Traces to P4-5: messages, status page and support view aligned on one status.
Synthesis paragraph; restates the thesis ('each promise came from the wrong place').
The seconds-versus-picking contrast and the day's slip are stated and their consequence given.
Eva's timeline is framed as 'this sequence' of the physical work; the day-late delivery is stated (its cause is deferred to Chapters ¶2, see flow results).
Figure 1's caption matches the timeline in the text (packed 14 April, delivered 15 April in Nijmegen, size L 19 April, exchange 22 April).
The volumes are explained as 'makes such promises at scale'.

The KEY POINTS bullets do not map onto the body's three rules: bullet 3 merges rule 1 (one writer) and rule 3 (one record), while the body's rule 2 carries the refund clause; 'stock that rises only on the warehouse's verdict' and 'every incident in this part is a promise made without its inputs' are not backed in the body. Both flow readers (A7, B7) could not map bullets to rules. The spec's own p04 grouping differs from the callout it cites as evidence.
results.quote: One writer per fact, one source per view.

results.finding: Figure 2's caption explains the systems picture (order record instructs, physical facts return as events to the one record read by notifications, status page and support agent). Note: the figure sits after the roadmap (¶5), not beside the rules (¶4) as the spec's evidence placement implies; readers still tied it to the rules.
The Queue That Waited is explained: spare picking capacity while orders never reached the warehouse.
Eva's case is explained: a fixed storefront rule ignored the missed 21:00 batch; the AC-2 reader reconstructed it. The rule itself is not quoted (see known_before_new).
The Store Stock Mirage is stated next to the till as the source of stock, so the reader can see the promise did not read the till; the link is implicit but no reader missed it.
Eva's exchange and the Double Refund are said to show why each action needs its own state and owner.
'Refund and restock wait for inspection, and one system issues refunds' is stated.
Eleven tickets explained by no system being able to say the order ships in two parcels.

Figure 3's caption introduces a 'four promises' frame the prose never sets up, and lists incidents in an order that pairs by position with promises that do not fit the text ('delivered tomorrow' with the Queue That Waited although the text ties the delivery-date promise to Eva; 'your order was delivered' with the Three-Status Order, a split-shipment problem). Both flow readers had to work the pairing out and the terms reader could not reconstruct it.
results.quote: the Queue That Waited, the Store Stock Mirage, the Three-Status Order and the Double Refund are the four made without them

results.finding: 'Eva's jacket order shows this sequence' expresses example.
'Eva bought from Kestrel & Pine' expresses elaboration of her order.
'At each step a system on the spot knows the facts first ... draws three rules from this' expresses cause_effect (flow reader B found it abstract; see flow results).
'The chapters follow Eva's parcel out and back' expresses sequence; it gives the order of the places, though it does not refer back to the rules explicitly.
The roadmap sentence at the end of the introduction announces the five places the section elaborates one by one.
'Then' expresses sequence from warehouse to carrier.
'Off Eva's route' expresses contrast with the parcel route.
'On the way back' expresses sequence to the return.
'Last' expresses sequence to the status chapter.

results.draft_locus: Chapters in this part ¶5 → Where to Begin ¶1
results.finding: 'None of these cases needed faster work; each promise came from the wrong place' sums up the cases (conclusion_summary).

Both flow readers describe the same organising principle as declared: hook, one case (Eva), company, rules, roadmap, chapters in the parcel's order (stores as a side branch), where to begin; both call the page easy to follow and keep the order; no section was unclear to both.

Flow A (item 7): the three-rules paragraph is hard to count; the second rule carries two ideas (computed promise and refund waiting for the bench), the refund clause reads as an example of rule one, and the rules do not line up with the KEY POINTS bullets.
results.quote: A promise such as a delivery date is computed from that writer's events, and a refund waits for the returns bench, where returns are inspected.

results.finding: Flow A (item 8): the roadmap claims the chapters follow Eva's parcel, yet lists stores as a leg, which the chapter list then calls 'Off Eva's route'.
results.quote: The chapters follow Eva's parcel out and back: warehouse, carrier and delivery date, stores, return and refund, and the status the customer sees.

results.finding: Flow A (item 9): Figure 3's 'four promises' appear for the first time, the incidents are in a different order from the chapters, and the positional pairing ('delivered tomorrow' with the Queue That Waited) contradicts the text; flow B called this the place it lost the thread most.
results.quote: The four promises of Part IV

results.finding: Flow A (item 10): KEY POINTS says every incident is a promise made without its inputs, but the chapter list describes the Queue That Waited as a backlog of orders that never reached the warehouse, not as a promise; the reader must supply the promise. Flow B (item 13) reports the same for the Queue That Waited.
results.quote: The Queue That Waited, a four-hour Black Friday backlog, shows why a warehouse can have spare picking capacity while customers wait for orders that never reached it.

results.finding: Flow A (item 11): 'it' has no clear referent; it took a moment to see it means the order.
results.quote: no system could say that it ships in two parcels

results.finding: Flow A (item 6): Duiven is called 'the warehouse' before the reader is told whose warehouse it is; the seller is named only in the next paragraph. Flow B (item 9) mentions the company-after-Eva order only as optional and not a problem, so this is not counted as corroborated.
results.quote: Duiven, the warehouse, picks and packs on 14 April

results.finding: Flow B (item 6): the paragraph gives the 21:14 order time and the day-late delivery but not why; the reader searched for the cause, which only appears in the shipping entry three paragraphs later. No forward pointer.
results.quote: PostNL delivers on Thursday 15 April, a day late.

results.finding: Flow B (item 8): after the company figures, 'At each step' is abstract; the reader had to go back to Eva's timeline to supply the steps.
results.quote: At each step a system on the spot knows the facts first.

results.finding: Flow A (item 12): 'faster work' contrasts with something the page never raised. (Flow B item 14 found 'faster work' follows on and objects instead to the wording 'wrong place'; the two readers disagree, so not corroborated.)
results.quote: None of these cases needed faster work

results.finding: Flow B (item 14): 'came from the wrong place' is new wording for what KEY POINTS and Figure 3 call 'made without its inputs'; the reader had to check they meant the same. (Flow A item 12 found this phrase works.)
results.quote: each promise came from the wrong place

results.finding: Known or glossed: system of record, single writer, events, order record, Waypoint and Kestrel & Pine (already_knows), returns bench (does_not_know, glossed in ¶4 'where returns are inspected'), Duiven, backlog (given by the Black Friday case), the incident names except the Three-Status Order, status page, messages and 'keyed by the return' (idempotency is known).
'pick wave' is on does_not_know and is never given; the body says 'picking batch' without linking the two (terms reader item 1).
results.quote: “Delivered tomorrow” needs the pick wave, the backlog and the carrier's transit time

results.finding: 'the work instruction and response' is on does_not_know and is named but never glossed; it is the first chapter's subject (terms reader item 4). The spec chose to name it only (decision log, length).
results.quote: the work instruction and response between order management and the warehouse

results.finding: 'the warehouse's verdict' (the disposition) is used before the body says what it is; the reader must infer it from 'Refund and restock wait for inspection' (terms reader item 8).
results.quote: stock that rises only on the warehouse's verdict

results.finding: 'The Three-Status Order' is not explained and clashes with the known 'three status lines' (terms reader item 13).
results.quote: The Three-Status Order drew eleven tickets

results.finding: 'collection' is used for both the carrier's pickup and customer collection in store, unglossed, in adjacent sentences; 'Collection schedules' in Chapters ¶2 is ambiguous (terms reader item 3).
results.quote: before the carrier's collection

results.finding: 'fixed storefront rule' is not stated, so the reader cannot see what the rule promised (terms reader item 11; the AC-2 reader raised the same doubt, but is not a flow reader).
results.quote: a fixed storefront rule

results.finding: 'location' is ambiguous: customer address, warehouse or store (terms reader item 12; also raised by the AC-2 reader).
results.quote: Collection schedules, backlog, location and carrier performance

results.finding: 'authorized owner' is vague next to the known 'single writer'; the reader cannot tell if it is the same idea (terms reader item 10).
results.quote: its own state and authorized owner

results.finding: Opens on a puzzling scenario (seconds-fast checkout against a day's slip), not on a scope statement, definition or 'this part explains'.
No weak pattern: not a bare summary, apology or new topic; it synthesizes the cases and gives a course of action.

Synthesis ('none needed faster work; each promise came from the wrong place') says what no chapter paragraph says of all cases, and the so-what (fix where promises read facts; start at the warehouse) follows.
'as did the opening's late delivery' and 'Eva's paid order reaches Duiven' call back to ¶1–¶2.

The cold reader of the introduction named five chapters in the roadmap's order: warehouse, carrier and delivery date, stores, returns and refunds (refund waits for inspection, single writer), the status the customer sees (one record for notifications, status page, agent). Against expected, the warehouse chapter was predicted as picking and stock ownership rather than the instruction and response, and the store chapter only partly as the till as a source; the subjects and order still match. The reader was unsure whether there are exactly five chapters.

The reader answered that a fixed storefront rule ignored that the 21:14 order missed Duiven's 21:00 last picking batch, and that the promise should be computed from the warehouse's batches and backlog, the carrier's collection schedule and performance, and the location; this matches expected. Doubts noted: the rule itself and PostNL's collection time are not stated.
